title: Level 6 · Object-Oriented Programming
blurb: Build your own types with classes, objects, inheritance and magic methods.

lessons.title: Classes
lessons.concept: A class is a blueprint that describes something: what it knows and what it can do. You write one with the class keyword and a name that starts with a capital letter. Things a class can do are written as methods: functions indented inside the class.
lessons.why: Real programs model things such as users, orders and games. Each one is a class.
lessons.example_note: Defines a Dog blueprint with one method and calls it.
lessons.prompt: Write a class Dog with a method speak(self) that returns the text 'Woof!'.
hints: Indent the method inside the class.
Every method's first parameter is self.
def speak(self): return 'Woof!'

lessons.title: Objects
lessons.concept: An object is one real thing built from a class: light = Light(). You can create many objects from one class, and each keeps its own data. Attach data to an object with a dot: light.state = 'on'.
lessons.why: A shop might have thousands of product objects, all built from one Product class.
lessons.example:
class Light:
    def describe(self):
        return 'The light is ' + self.state

a = Light()
a.state = 'on'
b = Light()
b.state = 'off'
print(a.describe())
print(b.describe())
lessons.example_note: Two objects from one class, each with its own state.
lessons.prompt: The class Light is given. Write a function make_light(state) that creates a Light(), sets its state and returns it.
hints: Create the object with Light().
Set light.state = state before returning.
light = Light(); light.state = state; return light

lessons.title: Constructors (__init__)
lessons.concept: Setting data after creating an object is tiring. The special method __init__ is the constructor: Python runs it automatically when you write Account('Asha', 100). Inside it, store the values with self.owner = owner.
lessons.why: Constructors make sure every object starts life with the data it needs.
lessons.example_note: The constructor stores the owner and balance.
lessons.prompt: Write a class BankAccount whose __init__(self, owner, balance=0) stores self.owner and self.balance. The balance defaults to 0.
hints: The constructor is named __init__ with two underscores each side.
Give balance a default value of 0.
self.owner = owner; self.balance = balance

lessons.title: Instance Variables
lessons.concept: Variables stored on self are instance variables: every object gets its own copy. If one student gets a mark, the other students are not affected. Create them inside __init__, including empty lists like self.marks = [].
lessons.why: Each customer, player or document must keep its own data separate from the others.
lessons.example:
class Student:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.marks = []

a = Student('Asha')
b = Student('Ravi')
a.marks.append(90)
print(a.marks, b.marks)
lessons.example_note: Only Asha's list changes; Ravi's stays empty.
lessons.prompt: Write Student(name) that stores self.name and an empty list self.marks. Add a method add_mark(self, mark) that appends the mark and returns self.marks.
hints: Use self.marks = [] inside __init__.
add_mark uses self.marks.append(mark).
Finish add_mark with return self.marks.

lessons.title: Class Variables
lessons.concept: A class variable is written directly inside the class (not in a method) and is shared by every object. Read it with ClassName.count or self.count. Use it for facts all objects share, like a company name or a counter of how many objects exist.
lessons.why: Counters, default settings and constants are shared across all objects of a class.
lessons.example:
class Employee:
    company = 'Rubitech'
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        Employee.count += 1

Employee('Asha')
Employee('Ravi')
print(Employee.company, Employee.count)
lessons.example_note: The shared counter goes up each time an Employee is created.
lessons.prompt: Write Employee(name) with a class variable company = 'Rubitech' and a class variable count = 0. Each time an object is created, add 1 to Employee.count.
hints: Class variables sit directly under the class line.
Inside __init__, write Employee.count += 1.
company = 'Rubitech' and count = 0 above __init__.

lessons.title: Instance Methods (self)
lessons.concept: An instance method is a function inside a class whose first parameter is self. Python passes the object in as self, so the method can read the object's data: self.width. You call it with a dot and no self: rect.area().
lessons.why: Methods let objects do work with their own data, like a cart totalling its own items.
lessons.example_note: area uses the object's own width and height.
lessons.prompt: The constructor of Rectangle is given. Add three methods: area(self), perimeter(self) and is_square(self) (True when width equals height).
hints: Each method takes self as the first parameter.
Read data with self.width and self.height.
perimeter is 2 * (self.width + self.height).

lessons.title: Class Methods (@classmethod)
lessons.concept: A class method works with the class itself instead of one object. Put @classmethod above it and name the first parameter cls. It is often used as an alternative constructor: cls(...) builds a new object.
lessons.why: Factories like Date.today() or User.from_json(text) are class methods.
lessons.example_note: Builds a Temperature from a Kelvin value.
lessons.prompt: Temperature(celsius) is given. Add a @classmethod called from_fahrenheit(cls, f) that returns cls(round((f - 32) * 5 / 9, 1)).
hints: Put @classmethod on the line above def.
The first parameter is cls, not self.
return cls(round((f - 32) * 5 / 9, 1))

lessons.title: Static Methods (@staticmethod)
lessons.concept: A static method belongs to the class's namespace but needs neither self nor cls. Put @staticmethod above a normal function. Use it for helper functions that are related to the class but do not touch any object's data.
lessons.why: Utility checks such as validating a password or converting units are often static methods.
lessons.example_note: Calls a helper on the class without creating an object.
lessons.prompt: Write a class PasswordCheck with a @staticmethod is_strong(password) that returns True when the password has at least 8 characters and contains at least one digit.
hints: Use @staticmethod and do not add self.
len(password) >= 8 checks the length.
any(ch.isdigit() for ch in password) checks for a digit.

lessons.title: Encapsulation (data hiding, _protected / __private, properties)
lessons.concept: Encapsulation means protecting an object's data. A single underscore (_x) says 'please do not touch', a double underscore (__x) makes the name private. Offer safe access with a @property, which lets you read acc.balance like a variable, and change data only through methods that check the rules.
lessons.why: Banks, games and shops must stop outside code from setting a balance to a nonsense value.
lessons.example_note: Cash is private but readable through a property.
lessons.prompt: Write Account(balance) with a private self.__balance and a read-only @property balance. deposit(amount) adds the amount and returns True only if amount > 0 (else False). withdraw(amount) subtracts and returns True only if 0 < amount <= balance (else False).
hints: Name the variable self.__balance and expose it with @property def balance(self).
Check the rule with an if before changing the balance.
deposit: if amount > 0: add and return True; otherwise return False.

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.concept: Inheritance lets a new class reuse an existing one. Write the parent in brackets: class Car(Vehicle):. The child gets all the parent's methods and data for free, and you only add what is new.
lessons.why: Instead of copy-pasting code for cars, bikes and trucks, you share it in a Vehicle parent.
lessons.example_note: Car uses info() from Vehicle and adds wheels().
lessons.prompt: Vehicle is given. Write Car(Vehicle) with wheels(self) returning 4, and Bike(Vehicle) with wheels(self) returning 2.
hints: Put the parent's name in brackets after the class name.
You do not need __init__ again; it is inherited.
class Car(Vehicle): def wheels(self): return 4

lessons.title: Multiple Inheritance
lessons.concept: A class can have more than one parent: class Duck(Swimmer, Flyer):. It then inherits abilities from all of them. Small parent classes that each add one ability are called mixins.
lessons.why: Mixing abilities (saveable, printable, loggable) in one class avoids duplicate code.
lessons.example_note: Duck gets swim and fly from two parents.
lessons.prompt: Swimmer and Flyer are given. Write Duck(Swimmer, Flyer) with a method abilities(self) that returns a list of self.swim() and self.fly().
hints: List both parents in the brackets, separated by a comma.
Inside abilities, call self.swim() and self.fly().
return [self.swim(), self.fly()]

lessons.title: Polymorphism
lessons.concept: Polymorphism ('many forms') means different classes can offer the same method name, each doing it in its own way. Code can then call shape.area() without caring whether it is a circle or a square.
lessons.why: Games call draw() on every character and payment systems call pay() on every method, without checking the type.
lessons.example_note: The same call speak() gives different results.
lessons.prompt: Write Circle(r) whose area() returns round(math.pi * r * r, 2), and Square(side) whose area() returns side * side. Then write total_area(shapes) that returns the rounded (2 decimals) sum of shape.area() for each shape.
hints: Both classes get a method with the same name: area.
total_area just loops and calls shape.area().
return round(sum(s.area() for s in shapes), 2)

lessons.title: Abstraction (abc, abstract classes)
lessons.concept: An abstract class is a template that cannot be used directly. Inherit from ABC (from the abc module) and mark required methods with @abstractmethod. Any child class must write those methods before you can create objects from it.
lessons.why: Abstract classes define a contract, like 'every payment method must have a pay() method'.
lessons.example_note: Square fills in the area() that Shape demands.
lessons.prompt: Make Shape an abstract class (inherit ABC) with an @abstractmethod area(self). Then write Rectangle(w, h) (area = w * h) and Triangle(b, h) (area = b * h / 2) as children of Shape.
hints: Write class Shape(ABC): and put @abstractmethod above area.
The abstract method body can just be pass.
Rectangle area is self.w * self.h; Triangle is self.b * self.h / 2.

lessons.title: Method Overriding
lessons.concept: Overriding means a child class writes a method with the same name as the parent's, so the child's version is used instead. The parent class itself stays unchanged.
lessons.why: A general Notifier can send a message, while email and SMS notifiers each send it their own way.
lessons.example_note: Pirate replaces hello() with its own version.
lessons.prompt: Notifier.send(msg) is given. Override send in EmailNotifier so it returns 'Email: ' + msg, and in SMSNotifier so it returns 'SMS: ' + msg.
hints: Use the exact same method name and parameters as the parent.
Return a different text in each child.
def send(self, msg): return 'Email: ' + msg

lessons.title: super()
lessons.concept: super() gives you the parent class. In a child's __init__, call super().__init__(...) so the parent sets up its part, then add the child's own data. This avoids repeating code.
lessons.why: Every framework class you extend (web pages, game sprites) expects you to call super().__init__().
lessons.example_note: The parent stores name; the child stores school.
lessons.prompt: Person(name) is given. Write Student(Person) with __init__(self, name, school) that uses super().__init__(name) and stores self.school. Add describe(self) returning name + ' @ ' + school.
hints: Call super().__init__(name) first.
Then set self.school = school.
describe returns self.name + ' @ ' + self.school

lessons.title: MRO (Method Resolution Order)
lessons.concept: When a class has several parents, Python must decide which parent's method to use. It follows the Method Resolution Order: the child first, then parents left to right, with shared ancestors last. See it with D.__mro__. So class D(B, C) checks B before C.
lessons.why: Understanding MRO explains surprising behaviour when mixing several parent classes.
lessons.example_note: Prints D, B, C, A, object in lookup order.
lessons.prompt: Write A with hello() returning 'A'; B(A) returning 'B'; C(A) returning 'C'. Then D(B, C) and E(C, B) with no methods of their own. Check which hello each one picks.
hints: D lists B first, E lists C first.
D and E need no body; use pass.
class D(B, C): pass  and  class E(C, B): pass

lessons.title: Composition
lessons.concept: Composition means an object has another object inside it, instead of being a kind of it. A Car has an Engine, so the Car stores an Engine in self.engine and asks it to do the engine's work.
lessons.why: 'Has-a' designs are flexible: you can swap an engine, a payment method or a logger without rewriting the whole class.
lessons.example_note: The Car owns an Engine and uses it.
lessons.prompt: Engine(hp) is given. Write Car(name, hp) that builds self.engine = Engine(hp) and stores self.name. Its start(self) returns name + ': ' + self.engine.start().
hints: Car does not inherit from Engine; it stores one.
self.engine = Engine(hp) inside __init__.
start returns self.name + ': ' + self.engine.start()

lessons.title: Magic Methods (__str__, __len__, __call__, __eq__ ...)
lessons.concept: Methods with double underscores on both sides are magic methods; Python calls them for you. __str__ controls str(obj) and print, __len__ controls len(obj), __eq__ controls ==, and __call__ lets you use the object like a function: obj(3).
lessons.why: Magic methods make your own classes feel built-in: printable, countable, comparable and callable.
lessons.example_note: print and len both use the magic methods.
lessons.prompt: Write Playlist(name, songs) (songs is a list). Add __str__ returning 'NAME (N songs)', __len__ returning the number of songs, __eq__(self, other) returning True when both songs lists are equal, and __call__(self, i) returning the song at index i.
hints: Each magic method has two underscores before and after its name.
__str__ must return text, e.g. f'{self.name} ({len(self.songs)} songs)'.
__eq__ compares self.songs == other.songs; __call__ returns self.songs[i].
